sources.news_title: Trump's own inner circle shocked by public execution plan: report
sources.text:
President Donald Trump's own inner circle was shocked by the news that he had signed off on Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth's order of public execution against Nidal Malik Hassan. It's America's first public execution in nearly a century.
"The idea seemed to shock even some of his colleagues in the administration," reported The New York Times' Peter Baker on Friday. "Vice President JD Vance cast doubt that it would be livestreamed, telling reporters that “I don’t know that that’s going to happen” and adding that he would not watch if it does."
Baker added, "But Mr. Trump said he signed off on it. 'Did I approve' he said. 'Absolutely I did.'" He pointed out that "no public execution has been conducted in the United States in 90 years, and the decision to conduct this one in front of an audience would put the country in the company of Afghanistan, Iran, North Korea and Somalia."
Baker also quoted a Republican lawmaker who, though outgoing, retains influence within the president's party in the Senate.
"Even some supporters of capital punishment flinched at the idea of livestreaming Mr. Hasan’s execution, calling it medieval and barbaric," Baker reported. "'Hasan should face the death penalty, but making his execution public and streaming it? Beyond disgusting,' said Senator Thom Tillis, Republican of North Carolina. 'Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do. It should not be happening in America.'"
Hasan murdered 13 people and injured 32 others at a military base in Fort Hood in Texas in 2009.
The outrage also came from conservatives and military professionals outside of the administration. On Thursday Billy Binion, reporter for the libertarian magazine Reason Magazine, wrote on X that “this is sick. You can support justice for Nidal Hasan’s victims without making his execution a source of entertainment. This administration so often governs for the online mob. It’s depraved.”
Glenn Greenwald, formerly of The Intercept and sometimes sympathetic to Trump, declared that “there are a very small number of countries that still carry out public executions. Those are the countries we are constantly told are uniquely primitive, barbaric, sick and evil. It’s revealing that Pete Hegseth wants the US to join that group but also entirely unsurprising.”
A retired intelligence officer, Travis Akers, argued that "this is vile. Does he deserve the death penalty? One million times yes and may he rot in h - - -. Should this be streamed for entertainment like the Romans throwing Christians to lions? Absolutely not." Other mental health experts who spoke with AlterNet described Trump as a "maniac" who appeals to racism and sexism.

JD Vance Says He 'Won't Be Watching' Fort Hood Killer's Execution

JD Vance Claims He 'Won't Be Watching' Fort Hood Killer's Execution — After Pete Hegseth Declared Death by Firing Squad Would Be 'Public'
Oct. 9 2026, Published 7:03 p.m. ET
Vice President JD Vance will not watch the planned execution of Nidal Malik Hasan if the Pentagon livestreams it, casting doubt on whether the public broadcast Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth described will take place at all, RadarOnline.com has learned.
"I don't know that that's actually going to happen," Vance told reporters. "If it's ultimately livestreamed, I'm not going to be watching it."
Pete Hegseth Believes the Public Execution Is a Deterrent
Hasan, a former Army major and psychiatrist, was convicted of killing 13 people and wounding 32 others in a shooting at Fort Hood, Texas, on Nov. 5, 2009.
President Trump approved the death sentence on October 2. Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle then directed that Hasan be executed by firing squad at Fort Hood at 1 p.m. Central Time on December 3.
Hegseth said on Thursday, October 8, that the execution would be carried out by a firing squad of soldiers and made available for the public to watch.
"People need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things," Hegseth said at the time.
JD Vance Wants to Refocus the Conversation
Vance, speaking while in Ohio, said he had seen the announcements and did not know whether a livestream would occur. He then turned to the underlying crime.
"This is a guy who committed, in my view, the worst terrorist attack on American soil outside of 9/11," the Veep said.
"The people that he was meant to treat, the Army soldiers that he was meant to treat for mental illness and other problems, he took them at their most vulnerable and gunned down these people where they lived."
He added that whatever the controversy over the method, people should not forget that Hasan "brutally murdered a lot of innocent people."
A military jury convicted Hasan in 2013 of 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of attempted premeditated murder and sentenced him to death.
He exhausted his military appeals, and the Supreme Court declined to review the case in March 2025.
Army regulations require the secretary of the Army to set an execution date between 60 and 150 days after presidential approval. Telle's October 6 directive placed the execution at the site of the 2009 attack.
Livestream Plans Have Drawn Criticism
The livestream plan has drawn criticism from both parties.
Some Republican lawmakers questioned the public broadcast, and the head of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops called the idea barbaric. Former officials have also warned that a livestream could serve as a recruiting tool for terrorists.
The last military execution was the hanging of Army Pvt. John Bennett on April 13, 1961. The last execution by a U.S. Army firing squad was that of Pvt. Eddie Slovik in 1945.

sources.text:
Vice President JD Vance expressed doubts about whether the firing squad execution of convicted Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan will be livestreamed, and indicated he would not watch if it is.
“Well, first of all, I see these announcements. I don’t know that that’s actually going to happen,” Vance told reporters during a campaign stop in Ohio on Oct. 9.
A day earlier, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth had indicated the plan was to make Hasan’s execution, scheduled for Dec. 3, viewable to the public.
The Pentagon subsequently confirmed it planned to livestream the execution, with more specific details still to come.
“This is a guy who committed, in my view, the worst terrorist attack on American soil outside of 9/11,” Vance told reporters. “Now, that said, I mean, look, if it’s through livestream, I’m not going to be watching it.”
Hasan was born in the United States and held the rank of major in the U.S. Army on the date of the Fort Hood shooting on Nov. 5, 2009.
Those killed in the 2009 shooting were 12 U.S. soldiers, a civilian physician, and an unborn child.
Thirty-two others sustained wounds during the attack.
During a 2013 military court-martial proceeding, Hasan identified himself as the shooter, described himself as a jihadist, and indicated he regretted his service in the U.S. military and had changed his allegiance.
The court-martial jury found Hasan guilty on 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of attempted premeditated murder, and recommended he be sentenced to death.
He has remained on the military’s death row at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas, ever since.
Hegseth announced the plan to publicize Hasan’s execution during an interview with Real America’s Voice host Jack Posobiec.
“He’s going to get a firing squad of soldiers, as it should be, and we'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things,” Hegseth told Posobiec.
Asked whether he was aware if Hasan had lodged any requests or appeals since learning of his execution details, Hegseth said, “Don’t care, we'll see him on Dec. 3.”
While Hasan’s military execution date is set for Dec. 3, he may be able to put off his death by firing squad through a habeas corpus appeal to the civilian federal court system and a request for a stay of execution.
Hasan would be the first U.S. military execution by firing squad since 1961.
While the United States has held public executions in the past, it has not been common practice for nearly a century. Legal scholars believe the last public execution in the United States occurred in 1936.
The human rights group Amnesty International documented 2,700 executions across 17 countries in 2025. Of that number, only Afghanistan and Iran had made those executions viewable to the public.
Amnesty International has opposed the death penalty, regardless of the underlying offense.
“Livestreaming the taking of a life by firing squad would only compound the cruelty of the death penalty and perpetuate the cycle of violence that the authorities purportedly seek to end,” Justin Mazzola, Amnesty International USA’s deputy director of research, said on Friday.

While US Vice President JD Vance—a Catholic convert—suggested on Friday that the administration may not actually livestream a firing squad execution at a military base in December, the church's top bishop in the country denounced the widely decried plan.
US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth pledged this week to make the execution of Fort Hood mass shooter Nidal Hasan "public," and officials said that would mean a livestream. As Religion News Service noted, the Pentagon chief is an evangelical Christian who has often spoken about his faith and "attends a church led by Pastor Doug Wilson, a self-described Christian nationalist."
On Friday, the vice president—who recently published a book about his religious experiences, including his conversion to Catholicism—told reporters that despite those statements about a livestream, "I don't know that that's actually gonna happen."
Vance argued that Hasan, a former Army major and doctor, committed "the worst terrorist attack on American soil outside of 9/11," but also said that "if it's ultimately livestreamed, I'm not gonna be watching it."
Meanwhile, using President Donald Trump's preferred term for the Department of Defense, Archbishop Paul Coakley, president of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops, said in a statement that "it is with shock and great sorrow that I have learned of the Department of War's decision to publicly livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan."
"Our God is the God of life. In no way can Hasan's actions be condoned, but this decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered. The word of God exhorts us: 'Do not repay anyone evil for evil' (Romans 12:17)," declared Coakley, a "conservative culture warrior" elected to his leadership role last year.
"The public execution even of one who has done grave harm will only further undermine the moral fabric of our nation and be a blight on the conscience of its people," he added. "I pray for the intercession of Our Lady of Good Counsel that we as a nation may always choose life even in the most trying times and circumstances."
Coakley joined a growing chorus of critics who have condemned the Pentagon plan, including the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, which said Friday that "the livestreaming of an execution is tantamount to a public execution and would breach the absolute prohibition of torture."
American Immigration Council senior fellow Aaron Reichlin-Melnick, who had blasted the livestream decision on Thursday, called the archbishop's statement a "strong response from the Catholic Church."
James Martin, a Jesuit priest and editor at large of America Magazine, explained that "the Catholic Church teaches that the death penalty is 'inadmissible,' primarily because every human being has God-given dignity, even a murderer, even a mass murderer. The televising of an execution is barbarism of the worst kind, offering up death as entertainment."
"Some Catholics still reject Pope Francis' magisterial pronouncement on the death penalty, which is now included in the Catechism," he noted. "But opposition to the death penalty, grounded in the respect for all human life, is not a brand new doctrine. Rather, it is one that took time to develop, as the church came to understand more deeply the innate dignity of every human life."
Sharing Coakley's comments on social media Friday, journalist Paul Blest wrote that "this happening so soon after the botched Tennessee execution is creating the conditions for real momentum against the death penalty."
Tennessee last week botched two attempts to kill Christa Pike with injections of pentobarbital, after which she was rushed to the hospital. Pike's legal team said Thursday that she "continues to experience cognitive challenges" but is taking "limited steps" with assistance. While Republican Gov. Bill Lee has responded by halting executions and ordering a probe, the incident has fueled fresh calls for the US to outlaw the death penalty at the state and federal level.
The Vatican's secretary of state, Cardinal Pietro Parolin, also weighed in on the livestream plan, saying Friday that "it is truly incomprehensible that anyone would want to use this method in this day and age. I do not know for what purpose. It is certainly unacceptable to turn death into a spectacle. However guilty the person may be, there are other ways."
"The church's position is one of total opposition to the death penalty. It is incompatible with human dignity and does not serve as a deterrent," Parolin said, acknowledging Coakley's comments and pledging that "there will be a statement from the Holy See."
As the Catholic leaders and others from various faiths spoke out against the Defense Department plan, Robert Jeffress, a Texas-based American Southern Baptist pastor and televangelist, wrote on social media that "I support the Pentagon's decision to livestream the execution of mass murderer Nidal Hasan. Capital punishment is commanded by God in Genesis 9:6 to remind people of the sanctity of human life. The more people that can see that truth illustrated through a public execution, the better."

Vice President JD Vance cast doubt Friday on whether the Pentagon will livestream the execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan in December but told reporters that if it is livestreamed, “I’m not going to be watching it.”
The Republican vice president said, “I don’t know that that’s actually going to happen,” when asked about the plans that the Pentagon confirmed Thursday. But Vance then tried to set aside the controversy over the shocking plans for a public execution and said Hasan’s crimes should not be forgotten.
Hasan was convicted of killing 13 people and injuring 32 others in a shooting spree at the military base in 2009.
“So whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don’t forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people,” Vance said.
“Now, that said, I mean, look, if it’s ultimately livestreamed, I’m not going to be watching it,” he added.
Vance is a convert to the Catholic Church, which has long opposed capital punishment.
Earlier Friday morning, the head of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops condemned the U.S. government’s decision to livestream Hasan’s execution.
“It is with shock and great sorrow that I have learned of the Department of War’s decision to publicly livestream the execution,” Archbishop Paul S. Coakley, president of the conference, said in a statement. He added that the decision was “a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered.”
Earlier, President Donald Trump told a White House event that Hasan will be getting “the death penalty through firing squad. And he deserves it.”
Trump, who approved Hasan’s execution, called him “a maniac.”
The president approved the method of execution by firing squad days after a failed attempt to execute Christa Pike by lethal injection late last month pushed Tennessee’s governor to halt further executions in that state this year.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the military hasn’t executed a service member by firing squad since World War II. The last military execution took place on April 13, 1961, when Army Pvt. John Bennett was executed by hanging.
Trump, who has long been a vocal supporter of capital punishment, didn’t mention the plans that the Pentagon has announced to livestream the execution so that the broader public can see it.
___
This story has been corrected to show the military base’s name is Fort Hood, not Ford Hood.

Vance says if livestream of Hasan’s execution happens, he’s ‘not going to be watching it’
The White House referred questions about the livestream to the Pentagon.
Vice President JD Vance said Friday that he wasn't sure whether there would be a livestream of Nidal Hasan's December execution, despite Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's confirmation of that plan, adding that if it were to be livestreamed, "I'm not going to be watching it."
"I don't know that's actually going to happen," Vance said when asked about the livestream of the execution of Hasan -- the former Army major who killed 13 people and wounded 32 others in a 2009 shooting at Fort Hood, Texas -- an attack Hasan described as an act of jihad. His execution would be the military's first since 1961 and its first by firing squad since 1945.
Vance later added that he hopes "people don't forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people."
"Now that said, I mean, look, if it's all through livestream, I'm not going to be watching it," he said.
While President Donald Trump supports the execution, it's still not clear whether the president agrees with Hegseth's plan to make it available to the public to watch.
Asked whether Trump supports the decision to make the execution available for public viewing, the White House referred ABC News to the Pentagon.
The Pentagon’s plan to livestream the execution of Hasan has drawn growing concerns among Republican lawmakers -- with many drawing a distinction between putting Hasan to death and allowing the public to watch it happen.
Joe Kent, a former senior Trump administration official who quit his post as director of the National Counterterrorism Center in March over the Iran war, warned that broadcasting Hasan's death could become a recruiting tool for terrorist groups.
In a social media post, Kent called the plan "beneath the dignity" of the United States, adding that, "Streaming his execution is not just a stain on our morality -- it also gives the terrorists free propaganda that they will use to radicalize & recruit more terrorists like Hassan."
Outgoing GOP Sen. Thom Tillis condemned the livestream plan Thursday as "beyond disgusting."
"Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do. It should not be happening in America," Tillis said.
Tillis, whose vote helped secure Hegseth's confirmation, recently described supporting him for Defense secretary as the "biggest regret of my career" in his new memoir.
Other Republicans echoed his objections, including Rep. Austin Scott, a member of the House Armed Services Committee.
"I absolutely support the sentence of death, but live-streaming executions is what jihadists do. America is better than that," Scott said in a statement on X.
Trump reiterated his support for executing Hasan by firing squad during remarks on Friday, but made no mention of broadcasting it. He framed the execution as part of his administration's broader effort to impose harsher criminal penalties.
"You know, today, if you get two days in jail -- today, you can do almost anything, nothing happens. But we're changing that, you see that. The death penalty through firing squad … and he deserves it. Killed and wounded many, many people, a maniac.” Trump said, without mentioning the livestream.
John Cohen, ABC News contributor and former Homeland Security official, said the visual of the U.S. military shooting a former member of the military "is a visual that will horrify some Americans and be exploited by our adversaries."
"As far as it serving as a deterrent to future attack -- for most terrorist -- martyrdom is the objective. Terrorist and other mass casualty attackers plan to and relish the thought of dying if it brings attention to their cause or grievance. So there is likely minimal deterrence an achieved by live-streaming," Cohen said.
Livestream announcement a surprise to some Army officials
Public executions were gradually outlawed by states beginning in the 19th century and have long been taboo across much of the developed world. They remain a practice in some authoritarian countries, including North Korea, where two nuclear researchers were reportedly executed publicly in early 2025 for failing to meet research expectations. Terrorist organizations also frequently use public executions as a means of intimidation.
Thursday’s announcement that Hasan’s execution would be livestreamed came as a surprise to some Army planners involved in the preparations, according to two officials with direct knowledge.
The decision to use a firing squad was also unexpected, according to a U.S. official familiar with the matter.
The Army had been preparing since at least February to potentially execute its four death row prisoners, including Hasan, but those plans centered on lethal injection at the federal prison in Terre Haute, Indiana, where the Justice Department carried out a series of civilian federal executions during Trump's first term, according to service documentation outlining the plans reviewed by ABC News.
Army planners are scrambling to develop procedures for carrying out an execution by firing squad, a method the service has not used since 1945, one official described. The Army's last written procedures for a firing squad execution date to 1959, leaving officials to determine how to adapt decades-old guidance for Hasan's execution.
Lethal injection had been the Army's only authorized method of execution since the 1980s, until a 2023 rule change gave the Army secretary broad discretion to determine how condemned prisoners would be put to death.
One priority for Army planners is protecting the identities of soldiers selected to carry out the execution, one official described. It remains unclear whether the soldiers would wear masks or what other measures the service might take to conceal their identities, particularly during a livestream.
The Army also has not publicly explained how it would handle a botched execution in which Hasan survives the initial volley. Procedures dating to 1959 call for the soldier commanding the firing squad to shoot the condemned prisoner in the head at point-blank range with a pistol if the initial shots fail to kill him.
It also remains unclear whether major online platforms, including YouTube, Facebook and X, would carry the execution livestream. None of the platforms responded to ABC News' request for comment.
The Pentagon routinely broadcasts its events through its own websites and social media accounts, but the platforms have rules governing graphic violence.

sources.news_title: Vance questions whether Pentagon will livestream execution of Fort Hood shooter
sources.text:
Vice President JD Vance was among a bipartisan group of politicians expressing concern and doubt over a Pentagon plan to livestream the execution of the former Army officer who killed fellow soldiers at Fort Hood, Texas.
“I don’t know that that’s actually going to happen,” Vance said Friday while taking questions from the press.
He was responding to comments Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and the Pentagon made Thursday announcing that the Dec. 3 execution of Nidal Hasan would be available for the public to watch through a livestream.
Hasan, an Army major and psychiatrist, opened fire in the early afternoon at Fort Hood’s Soldier Readiness Processing Center on Nov. 5, 2009. Witnesses said he shouted “Allahu akbar,” which is Arabic for “God is great.”
He was found guilty of killing 13 people and injuring more than 30 and sentenced to death in a court-martial in 2013.
Hasan, now 56 and paralyzed from the waist down, is scheduled for execution by firing squad at 1 p.m. Central time on Dec. 3 at Fort Hood, according to a memo from acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle.
Public executions are not part of the modern American justice system, with the last taking place in 1936. When the federal government executed Timothy McVeigh, who carried out the 1995 bombing of a government building in Oklahoma City, it did allow for survivors and victims to watch him die by lethal injection via a closed-circuit telecast, according to a report from National Public Radio.
The last service member executed by the military was Army Pvt. John A. Bennett, who was hanged at Fort Leavenworth in 1961 after being convicted of the rape and attempted murder of an 11-year-old girl.
The Army’s last known execution by firing squad dates to 1945, when Pvt. Eddie Slovik was shot by firing squad in France after being convicted of desertion.
Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., said that Hasan should face the death penalty but that streaming it to the public is “beyond disgusting.”
“Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do. It should not be happening in America,” he said in a statement on social media.
Sen. Jack Reed, D-R.I., a retired Army officer, said the decision makes Hasan’s death sentence a “barbaric spectacle” and called for the administration to reconsider this plan because it gives the shooter more attention and control.
“Instead of forcing the shooter to face justice, the Trump administration is literally handing him more power and offering him a global platform to amplify his hateful, anti-American message. This is a gift to anti-American terrorist recruiters. It is absolutely shameful and damaging to America’s interests and core values,” he said in a statement posted to social media.
Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., a retired Navy captain, said that Hegseth should be removed from his job because of the plan. Sen. Mazie Hirono, D-Hawaii, called on him to resign. She is also a senior member of the Senate Armed Services Committee.
“How about they trade glorifying violence for solving some problems and delivering for the American people? We need to be reminded of the nation we can be at our best,” Kelly said in a post on social media.
Hirono said Hasan must face justice “but giving him a public platform to spew hate only hands extremists a powerful tool for anti-American recruitment and radicalization.”
“The United States cannot stoop to a level of grotesque violence frequently used by the terrorist organizations United States service members have fought so hard against,” she said.
The Pentagon said it had nothing to provide when asked for comment on the criticism.
If the plan does go forward, Vance said he does not intend to watch.
“Whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don’t forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people,” he said.

sources.text:
US V-P Vance does not know if Pentagon will proceed with live-stream of Fort Hood gunman’s execution
WASHINGTON - Vice-President J.D. Vance said on Oct 9 he does not know whether the Pentagon will proceed with a livestream of the execution by firing squad of the former US Army psychiatrist convicted in the deadly 2009 Fort Hood shooting, a plan that has drawn broad condemnation.
Several Republican lawmakers criticised the move championed by Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, while a top US Catholic bishop called the plan “barbaric” and former US officials said a live-stream of the execution would hand terrorists a recruiting tool.
“I don’t know that that’s actually going to happen,” Vance told reporters in Cincinnati, referring to a live-stream.
Vance added that if a livestream of the execution scheduled for Dec 3 occurs, “I’m not going to be watching it.”
The No. 2 US official’s comments raise questions about the extent of opposition within President Donald Trump’s administration to the Pentagon’s plans to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, who was found guilty in a US military trial of killing 13 people at Fort Hood in Texas.
Trump said at a White House event that Hasan deserves the death penalty by firing squad, calling him “a maniac.”
The Republican president has not said whether he thinks the event should be shown on a live-stream.
A senior White House official familiar with the matter said that Trump “doesn’t oppose the idea” of a live-stream of the execution, but that his position is not yet final and he could change his mind.
The White House is hearing concerns from lawmakers, allies and religious leaders who are urging the administration to not live-stream the execution, the official said, speaking on condition of anonymity.
Death penalty experts said it would mark the first known broadcast or live-stream of a lawful execution.
‘For all to see’
Hegseth, a Trump appointee, said on Oct 8 the public nature of the execution would demonstrate “there’s serious consequences for these types of things.”
Hegseth reposted a comment Trump made in 2013, possibly about the Boston Marathon bombers, saying: “Should be public execution for all to see – you will end this bull**** fast!”
The Pentagon on Oct 9 declined to say whether families of those killed in Hasan’s attack would be invited to attend the execution, as is common practice in civilian executions.
It remains unclear how the Army would select the shooters and what protocols might be followed during the execution itself. The Pentagon said it would release details later.
A top US Catholic official condemned the plan.
“This decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered,” said Archbishop Paul Coakley, president of the United States Conference of Catholic Bishops.

Pete Hegseth has drawn intense criticism and calls for him to be removed as Defense Secretary after announcing that Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan’s execution by firing squad would be “made public.”
A slew of Democrats and at least two Republicans have condemned the prospect of live-streaming the death, calling it “medieval,” “disgusting” and reminiscent of a dictatorship.
Hegseth told conservative outlet Real America’s Voice Thursday that Americans would be able to watch the execution of Hasan, an Army psychiatrist convicted of killing 13 people and injuring 32 others at the Texas Army base in 2009.
“We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public because people need to understand there are serious consequences for these types of things,” the secretary said. The Pentagon confirmed to The Independent that the execution, scheduled for December 3 at Fort Hood, will be live-streamed and that more details would be provided soon.
While many lawmakers said Hasan should indeed face his capital sentence, they condemned the prospect of broadcasting his state-sanctioned killing, casting it as barbaric.
“Hasan should face the death penalty, but making his execution public and streaming it? Beyond disgusting,” Senator Thom Tillis, a North Carolina Republican, wrote on X. “Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do. It should not be happening in America.”
“I absolutely support the sentence of death, but live-streaming executions is what jihadists do,” Rep. Austin Scott, a Georgia Republican, posted on X. “America is better than that.”
Numerous Democrats voiced similar objections. “I mean, that’s disgusting,” Senator Chris Murphy, a Connecticut Democrat, told CNN. “What is he mimicking? ISIS executions.”
Senator John Ossoff, a Georgia Democrat, sharply criticized Hegseth and described the idea of a live streamed execution as an “obscene medieval spectacle.” In an interview with MS NOW, he called Hegseth a “deeply unwell person who seems to relish this kind of brutality.”

Kelly, a retired Navy Captain, also called on the defense secretary to be “removed immediately.”
Some Republicans have applauded Hegseth’s decision. Tennessee Rep. Andy Ogles wrote on X: “Excellent. Public execution is what this terrorist deserves. We will be watching.”
On Thursday, Hegseth said the U.S. military had not executed a service member by firing squad since World War II. “I kind of like the mentality we had in World War II, which was [to] win,” the defense secretary said.
The last person executed by a U.S. military firing squad was Army Private Eddie Slovik, who faced 12 riflemen from his own unit on January 31, 1945.
Hegseth recommended that Hasan be executed by firing squad, and President Donald Trump approved the request earlier this month. The defense secretary called the decision a “no brainer.”
When asked on Thursday if Hasan, 56, had made any final requests, Hegseth said: “Don’t care. We’ll see him on December 3.”
Hasan, an Army major who was scheduled to deploy to Afghanistan in 2009, was convicted by a military jury of 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of attempted premeditated murder. He was sentenced to death in 2013.

Vice-President JD Vance has ignited fierce political controversy after asserting that socialism had become 'a hard term to define these days' before offering an unorthodox interpretation linking the philosophy directly to foreign labour replacement and transgender athletes.
The remarks came at a White House press conference on Thursday, 8 October 2026, where Vance announced that Microsoft and Adobe had been suspended from the PERM labour certification programme.
The exchange circulated widely on X. Critics accused him of emptying the word of meaning as Republicans make attacks on socialism central to their midterm campaign.
With Republicans placing attacks on democratic socialists at the heart of their legislative strategy, the controversial press conference highlights how cultural grievances and immigration enforcement have become inextricably intertwined in the final weeks of the campaign trail.
'I Don't Know What the Term Means Anymore'
A reporter asked Vance how he personally defined socialism. 'It's a hard term to define these days,' he began. 'Classically, you would think socialism is about prioritising workers.'
He then turned to the announcement he had just made. Most self-described socialists running for office, he said, 'are going to howl about this announcement today, which is prioritising American workers over foreign workers. So I don't know what the term means anymore.'

'That's what unites the socialists that I see running across the United States of America today.'
He cited Senator Bernie Sanders's comments on open borders during the 2016 presidential campaign as an example. Neither position defines socialism, which is generally understood as an economic system in which the means of production are owned or controlled collectively.
A Clip Viewed Millions of Times
Independent journalist Aaron Rupar posted the exchange on X shortly after the event. The clip had been viewed more than 3.8 million times as of Friday.
Ed Krassenstein, a political commentator, was among those who seized on it. 'He claims it traditionally means "prioritising workers", but today it means "boys playing girls' sports" and "replacing American workers with foreign workers",' he wrote, before adding an insult about the vice-president's intelligence.
Some replies to Rupar's post criticised Vance's answer. One response, which had more than 20,000 likes, mocked Vance's definition as 'anything I can say that will scare' his supporters.
Malcolm Ferguson, writing in The New Republic, called the answer a dodge from a politician whose public image has often emphasised intellectual sophistication.
He noted that socialism carries a range of meanings, from the dignified standard of living promised by New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani to classical models centred on redistributing wealth from elites to workers.

The question came at an event for the administration's Anti-Fraud Task Force, which Vance leads. Microsoft disputed his characterisation. The company said 'the vast majority of Microsoft employees in the United States are Americans' and that it pays H-1B employees the same as others doing comparable work.
Labor Department Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito announced an investigation into alleged J-1 visa fraud involving nine universities, including Harvard, Yale, Stanford and MIT. An investigation is not a finding that any of the institutions acted unlawfully.
The timing was awkward. On the same day, Donald Trump presented Microsoft chief executive Satya Nadella with the National Medal of Technology and Innovation.
Vance acknowledged the timing at the press conference. He called Microsoft 'a great American company' and said the administration would maintain a good relationship with it, while continuing to deny its permanent residency applications until it put American workers first. Attorney General Todd Blanche said the Justice Department was investigating companies that discriminate against American workers in favour of foreign hires.
A Midterm Message Under Strain
Vance and Trump have sought to frame the 3 November midterms as a contest against socialism, as Vance did in August while Republicans faced difficult polling. Zohran Mamdani, a democratic socialist elected mayor of New York City in 2025, has become a frequent target of Republican attacks.
Thursday's answer gave opponents a different line of attack. By defining socialism through immigration and transgender athletes, Vance fed a long-running Democratic complaint that Republicans use the word as a catch-all label rather than a description of economic policy.
The vice-president has made opposition to transgender athletes competing in women's sports and restrictions on skilled immigration recurring themes of his speeches.
The remarks came less than four weeks before the 3 November midterm elections, as Republicans continued to make opposition to socialism a central theme of their campaign.

“I don’t find peace in that. My peace comes from my faith,” Willingham said about the upcoming execution.
Other survivors have described the emotional difficulty of returning to Fort Hood nearly 17 years after the shooting. Some intend to attend the execution, while others prefer not to witness another death.
There are also unresolved legal questions surrounding the Fort Hood execution.
According to the Associated Press, Hasan could still file a habeas corpus petition in civilian federal court challenging his detention or sentence. Such a filing could delay the scheduled execution substantially.
Military legal experts have also questioned the procedures surrounding the firing squad and the notification process.
For now, the December 3 date remains scheduled, and the Pentagon’s livestream announcement remains in place despite Vance’s uncertainty.

US plan for public firing squad execution sparks controversy
Digital Desk |
New York, Oct 9 (IANS) US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has announced that a convicted terrorist would be executed publicly through livestreaming when he is killed by a firing squad, sparking controversy over making it a public spectacle.
“We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public,” he said of the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, an Army psychiatrist who was convicted in the terrorist killing of 13 people at a military base in 2009.
The Pentagon said on Thursday that the execution would be livestreamed.
This would be the first public execution in the US in about a century, returning to a practice now found only in repressive regimes such as those in Afghanistan, Iran and North Korea, as well as the terror group Islamic State when it controlled territories before its rout.
Even Saudi Arabia, which used to make a public spectacle of beheadings, has discontinued the practice of conducting them openly.
United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres' Spokesperson Stephane Dujarric criticised the planned public display on Friday, describing it as “abhorrent”.
“A government executing someone in public or in front of live cameras, frankly, is abhorrent,” he said.
The move was also criticised by leaders of President Donald Trump's own party as unbecoming of the US.
Republican Senator Thom Tillis called the plan “beyond disgusting”, pointing out that “public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do”.
Austin Scott, a senior Republican member of the House Armed Services Committee, said: “Live-streaming executions is what jihadists do.”
“America is better than that,” he added, while also saying that he supported the death penalty.
Hasan's conviction was by court-martial, as he was an Army major. If he is executed, it would be the first military execution since 1961 and the first public execution in the US since World War II.
He did not contest his conviction, readily conceding that he carried out the shooting, which also wounded 32 people, as a “mujahideen”.
He had also sent a communication to Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi, the late self-proclaimed “Caliph” of the Islamic State.
Except for federal and military cases, the death penalty falls under state laws, with some states carrying out large numbers of executions, while 23 of the 50 states have abolished it.
The methods of execution also vary, with some states allowing the electric chair, firing squads, or lethal injections.
According to the Death Penalty Information Center, 47 people were executed in 11 states last year.
The death penalty has raised questions in the US after Tennessee state's attempt to execute a woman reportedly failed when two lethal injections did not kill her this week, and she is now in the hospital.
The case of Linda Pike, who survived the execution attempt, is unusual because she was sentenced in 1995 for the murder of an acquaintance when she was 18 years old and had been on death row for more than 30 years.
The man who carried out the murder with her was spared the death penalty because he was under 18 years old.
